which sets out regulations and licensing requirements for taxis and transportation network companies.
Administration is aware of several operational issues and inefficiencies related to taxis,
which could be approved through by law amendments.
Engagement with the taxi industry, including taxi brokerages, taxi license owners, taxi drivers,
and union leadership was conducted to discuss these issues and how they could be addressed.
To help inform these meetings, administration conducted a municipal scan of Western Canadian cities.
As a result of the findings of the municipal scan and industry engagement,
administration is recommending the standing policy committee on transportation,
recommend eight by law amendments to city council.
Number one, remove requirements for proof of broker affiliation for a taxi driver license application.
This is no longer necessary as taxi brokers submit applications on behalf of their drivers.
Number two, establish a minimum number of five affiliated taxis to qualify for a new broker license.
Currently there is no minimum number of affiliated taxis required.
However, brokers are required to provide service 24 hours a day and 70 is a week.
Establishing a minimum number of affiliated taxis will ensure brokerages are large enough to meet these operating requirements.
Number three, permit taxis to display an SGI breakdown permit in lieu of the city of Saskatoon taxi license when temporarily transferring the taxi license to a different vehicle.
Currently taxi owners are required to purchase and display a new taxi plate deckle from the city.
This results in taxis being out of service when collisions occur outside of city hall hours.
Number four, increase the cleaning fee that is charged when a passenger soils at taxi from $100 to up to $200.
Number five, required taxis to utilize broker issued tax equipment such as debit and credit card machines and in car cameras.
Cameras would also be required to record for a minimum of four days.
Number six, remove provisions related to mechanical taxi meters as these are no longer in use and replace with language referring to digital taxi meters.
Number seven, require all taxes to display a city issue deckle showing fairs and other bylaw information.
Fairie deckles are currently required but are provided by taxi brokers and are not standardized across brokerages.
And lastly, number eight, convert the current van rate fair structure to a large vehicle fair.
The existing van rate was introduced in 2005 when vans transport five or more passengers or more luggage them look in fitness sedan.
The fare at the end of the trip is multiplied by 1.5 times.
Only vans may charge this rate. Other passenger vehicles such as larger SUVs are excluded.
In 2005, they were very few vans in the taxi fleet resulting in van taxis traveling significant distances to reach their passengers at the start of the fare.
This combined with higher capital and operating expenses compared to sedan's necessitated a van rate fair structure that would appropriately compensate the driver of taxi vans.
Concerns have been raised with a administration about driver discretion in charging the van rate by determining roadside whether the passenger's luggage could have fit in a sedan.
This is resulted in the perception from some residents that the van rate could be misupplied and is overly complex.
There have been many changes to taxi services since the van rate was adopted in 2005.
Amendments are needed to ensure the additional compensation providing large vehicle service is aligned with current expenses and practices.
Vantaxis are more common now than they were in 2005.
44% of the taxi fleet is currently vans, which means vans are no longer needed to travel as far to reach their passengers.
Due to technological advancements, the most popular van taxi vehicles achieve similar fuel economies as sedans and have similar operating expenses.
However, vans continue to have high capital purchase costs compared to sedans.
Saskatoon has significantly grown over this period as well.
The current van rate 1.5 multiplier on a long taxi trip results in disproportionately high taxi fares.
Municipal scanners found that van rate multipliers are not best practices and more cities are using flat rates or no additional charges at all.
In consideration of this, administration is proposing converting the van rate 1.5 multiplier to a large vehicle fare of $9.50.
This would be applicable on all vehicles, men.

And you fact should deceit five or more passengers. And be charged only when the vehicle is requested by a passenger through taxi dispatch. The proposed large vehicle fair will continue to address the additional capital expenses of the van. Open the fair to a wider variety of vehicle types. Align Saskatoon's regulations more closely with other cities. And remove driver discretion in assessing the amount of luggage roadside. Simplifying the fair structure and improving predictability for passengers. Engagement on this item was mixed.

Taxi brokers were supportive of this amendment while union leadership which represents most drivers were supportive of the change with the added caveat that drivers continue to have to have the discretion to charge the fair roadside based on the amount of luggage and number of passengers.
